background.definition: Passage of 3 or more unformed stools over 24 hours, occurring with or without additional symptoms of fever, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping, which occurs in persons traveling outside of their usual country of residence. Updated guidelines for traveler's diarrhea from an expert panel define mild diarrhea as tolerable, moderate as distressing, and severe as incapacitating or completely disruptive of planned activities.

list.listitem: The highest risk of diarrhea occurs when visiting tropical countries with poor sanitation. Destinations with the highest risk include South Asia and West/Central Africa.
Incidence is influenced by the quality, type, and location of food consumption.
Diarrhea is the most common health problem in travelers, affecting approximately 40% of travelers. Studies show an overall decline in the incidence of traveler's diarrhea over the past 20 years.

According to GeoSentinel (a global surveillance system) the most common post-travel diagnoses included unspecified diarrhea (8%), acute bacterial diarrhea (5%), post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome (5%), Giardia (3%) and chronic unknown diarrhea (3%).

A systematic review of cohort studies identified 10 studies with 8478 travelers from high income countries. The pooled incidence of mild diarrhea was 24%, of moderate diarrhea was 8% and of severe diarrhea was 3%. Risk factors for traveler's diarrhea include backpacking, low and middle income destinations, and younger age.
A wide range of infectious organisms, including bacteria, viruses, and parasites, can cause diarrhea.

Bacteria transmitted by contaminated food or water cause the majority of cases; enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) is the most common, followed by enteroaggregative E. coli, Campylobacter, Salmonella, and Shigella.

Epidemiology varies depending on the location and season of the year. Travelers from industrialized nations visiting developing countries are more likely to ingest enteropathogens because of inadequate public health practices.
Diarrhea can happen in backcountry backpackers hiking in the US.
Risk factors include drinking untreated surface water (odds ratio [OR] = 2.4) and rinsing utensils in untreated water (OR = 1.9), and staying in accommodations without running water or refrigeration.
A stool pathogen cannot be identified in over a third of patients.
Travelers ingest food or water contaminated by the organism or its toxins.
Bacteria attach to the intestinal mucosa and release enterotoxins or cytotoxins.
Enterotoxins bind a specific receptor to penetrate into the cells and induce an increase of fluid secretion.
Cytotoxins disrupt intestinal mucosa.
The risk of contracting traveler's diarrhea may be reduced by proper selection of food and drinks. C
Both bismuth subsalicylate and antibiotics help prevent traveler's diarrhea, A but routine use of antibiotic prophylaxis is not advised. C

Educate patients about proper food hygiene and the avoidance of drinking untreated water prior to travel. However, studies have not demonstrated a significant reduction in traveler's diarrhea with patient education.
Use of an alcohol-based hand sanitizer reduces the risk of acquiring an infectious cause of diarrhea and vomiting.

Taking bismuth subsalicylate 2 oz. or 2 tablets 4 times daily during travel provides 65% protection from developing diarrhea. A systematic review of 14 studies found that taking bismuth subsalicylate had an odds of 3.5 for preventing traveler's diarrhea.
Prophylactic antibiotics effectively prevent diarrhea but are not recommended for most travelers because of side effects, expense, and risk of resistant bacteria.

Consider prescribing prophylactic antibiotics in patients with an underlying medical condition that makes the consequences of dehydration severe, such as severe inflammatory bowel disease; severe vascular, cardiac, or renal disease; advanced HIV; and after organ transplant. A fluoroquinolone antibiotic should be given for no more than 2 to 3 weeks (see for recommended prophylactic antibiotics).
Poorly absorbed antibiotics, such as rifaximin, may cause fewer adverse effects and less chance of resistance, while decreasing diarrhea in travelers.
Some strains of probiotics, such as S. boulardii, may reduce the risk of traveler's diarrhea.Probiotics should be started 2 days before leaving and continued throughout travels.
Vaccines

Two typhoid vaccines (one oral and one injectable) are licensed in the US and only recommended when there is moderate to high risk of exposure to Salmonella enterica species and laboratory personnel and researchers at risk for expoure.
IDSA guidelines recommend a live attenuated single dose oral cholera vaccine for adults 18–64 years of age who travel to cholera-affected areas.
Current trials are evaluating the safety of a potential vaccine against ETEC.
Usually no need to diagnose the specific etiology. C
Traveler's diarrhea is usually a diagnosis made by the patient.
Patients traveling abroad or camping typically present with diarrhea with or without malaise, low-grade fever, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps.
Most episodes occur between 4 and 14 days after arrival. The illness is usually self-limited, lasting 1 to 5 days.
Consider enteric fever in persons who have travelled to parts of the world where salmonella typhi and paratyphi are endemic.
No tests are recommended for most cases of traveler's diarrhea.
Send stool testing if the traveler has a fever, blood in the stool, or severe abdominal pain.
Send an examination for ova and parasites and antigen detection for Giardia and Cryptosporidium species if diarrhea persists beyond 10 to 14 days.
When enteric fever or bacteremia are suspected, order cultures and multiplex PCR from stool and blood.
Traveling patients typically present with diarrhea with or without malaise, low-grade fever, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps.
Only send stool testing (culture or molecular-based technique) if the traveler has fever or blood in the stool, and send stool for ova and parasites only if symptoms are prolonged.
Management of traveler's diarrhea includes prompt self-treatment in case of illness. A
Self-treatment consists of fluid replacement, a short course of an antibiotic in moderate-to-severe cases, and bismuth subsalicylate or loperamide for control of diarrhea if necessary. A
Travelers should seek medical care if high fever, bloody stools, or worsening abdominal pain develops for consideration of antibiotics. C

A short course (single dose to 3 days) of an antibiotic shortens the duration and severity of diarrhea. Consider giving travelers a prescription for an antibiotic that can be taken if moderate-to-severe diarrhea develops. See for recommended antibiotics for treatment of moderate-to-severe traveler's diarrhea. See

A fluoroquinolone antibiotic (or alternatively azithromycin) is recommended as first-line therapy by IDSA guidelines (2017) for traveler's with fever or signs of bacteremia. Azithromycin is recommended for persons traveling to Southeast Asia, where ciprofloxacin-resistant Campylobacter species are present. For infants < 3 months a 3rd generation cephalosporin is recommended.

May use bismuth subsalicylate in mild cases and loperamide for moderate-to-severe diarrhea when fever and bloody stools are absent. It is unclear if taking loperamide with an antibiotic offers significant benefits.
SP 303 (Provir), a plant-derived product with antisecretory properties, shortens the duration of traveler's diarrhea.
A Cochrane review concluded that probiotics are probably not effective for treatment of acute diarrhea.

Advise patients to promptly begin self-treatment if traveler's diarrhea develops. Most importantly, maintain hydration through drinking broth or fruit juice in mild cases and the use of oral rehydration packets in severe illness. Most cases are self-limited and resolve within a few days with hydration only.

While oral rehydration solution (ORS) for acute watery diarrhea is usually glucose based, polymer based ORS prepared with wheat or rice may be superior because it more slowly releases glucose. A Cochrane review found low quality evidence that suggested an 8 hour reduction in the duration of diarrhea and a small reduction in stool volume with polymer based ORS.
A single dose of an antibiotic is as effective as a 3-day course.
A traveler may complete a 3-day course if he/she is not well at 24 hours after starting the antibiotic.
Advise travelers to seek medical care if symptoms worsen or fail to improve within 48 hours of initiating antibiotics.
Traveler's diarrhea is usually a self-limited illness that resolves spontaneously within 1 to 5 days. C
3% to 17% of travelers who experienced diarrhea develop post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome. B
Routinely wash hands with soap and water after toileting.
Do not swallow water while bathing or showering.
Disinfect water if camping.
Drink bottled water, soft drinks without ice, or hot tea or coffee.
Eat hot, thoroughly cooked foods and fruits and vegetables peeled by the traveler.
Consider taking daily prophylactic bismuth subsalicylate.
May take loperamide or bismuth subsalicylate for control of diarrhea if it interferes with travel plans.
Seek medical care if you develop high fever, bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, or no improvement with antibiotics.
Avoid treatment with fluoroquinolones.
